A user starts the yearly sales export, waits ten seconds and closes the tab. The endpoint takes a

, so the team assumes the work stops when the client leaves. The logs say otherwise: the server keeps sending all twelve monthly queries to the sales service and builds a CSV that nobody will ever download. On a busy day, abandoned exports pile up and slow down everyone else. The token was accepted, and then ignored.
works like a remote kill switch. Pass one into a method, call
somewhere else, and the method stops right there, whatever it was doing.
It's easy to see why. The names suggest it:
, and ASP.NET Core hands every endpoint a token tied to the request. Built-in methods like
really do stop quickly when the token you pass them is canceled, so cancellation seems automatic. And if you come from older .NET Framework code,
really could stop a thread from the outside.
But a token is only a signal. Something on the other side has to look at it.
The source signals, the token listens
creates the token and is the only object that can cancel it. The token itself is a small struct you pass to whoever should listen; every copy observes the same source. When you call
and can never go back to
, the token's wait handle is signaled, and callbacks registered with
returns. That's the whole list. No running code is interrupted, no thread is stopped.
Why .NET doesn't just stop the work
Stopping code at an arbitrary instruction is dangerous: a lock may stay held, a file may be left half-written, a static constructor may never run. That's why
on .NET Core and .NET 5+, and why Microsoft recommends a
, the requester only asks. The code doing the work decides where it's safe to stop: after the current row, after rolling back a transaction, or not at all once a step is past the point of no return.

What "canceled" looks like to the caller
There are two ways for cooperative code to stop. It can simply return, but then its task ends as
and the caller can't tell it was cut short. Or it can throw
does. An async method that throws it ends in the
state, and awaiting that task throws the exception again, so the caller knows exactly what happened. Either way, some work may still finish after
is called: cancellation takes effect at the next check, not at the next instruction.

content.text: How to apply it in your project

items.title: Accept a token in every slow async method

content.text: Any method that does I/O or long-running work should take a
, conventionally as the last parameter. In ASP.NET Core, endpoints and controller actions can simply declare one.
Pass the token to every method that accepts it. Analyzer rule CA2016 finds the calls you missed; it's enabled as a suggestion in .NET 10, which is easy to overlook.
In CPU-bound loops or batch jobs, call
once per item or batch, so a canceled job stops within one unit of work.
